This skill turns a conversation with the owner into a hyp tree that an unattended `/goal` run can finish: a Goal with its lines, the contested questions under it with their rivals, and nothing the run must come back to ask. It ends where the hyp-goal-run skill starts. Use it with the hyp-prototype skill for the commands that add nodes.

The grill is not done when the owner and you agree. It is done when every question is in its place in the tree, the owner approved each owner write, and nothing is left that only the owner can answer.

## Start

1. Find the store. Run `hyp status` at the repository root. A new purpose in a repository that has a store is a new Goal **in the same store**: one store holds many Goals. If the installed hyp refuses a second Goal in one log, the new Goal is a new tree under its own directory. Run `hyp init` only when there is no store.
2. Set `HYP_ACTOR` to a runner name unique to this session. Ask the owner for their actor name (lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, for example `owner-dat`) once.
3. Read the glossary of the repository, if it has one. Use its words. One concept gets one word, and every sense of the word has one shape. Before you name a thing by how it is stored (`bases`, `commits`), look for the domain word.

## Rounds

Work in rounds. A round asks every question whose prerequisites are settled, numbered, each with your recommendation. Wait for the answers, then compute the next round.

Every question opens with what exists today and the problem it settles, then gives one small worked example of each option and the principle behind it. A choice without its basis is not a question the owner can answer. Name why each mechanism is in the question; if you cannot, drop it.

Run the mistakes checklist below on each round before you send it, and again before Confirm the routing.

## Mistakes checklist

Each item is a mistake earlier grills made. Check the round or the table against every item, and fix what fails before the owner sees it.

1. **Store.** The Goal goes where the repository's agent instructions (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) say trees live, such as `investigations/<topic>/`: in the store there that holds the Goal of the issue's parent issue, when one does, or else in a new store in that directory. No `hyp init` at the repository root unless the instructions name no directory for trees.
2. **Test method.** Where an installed skill owns the test method (for a skill, ak-skill-creator's eval flow: its cases, fixtures, matching and grading), the round asks only whether to use that flow and the owner's preferences of model, trial count and budget, never a choice among the method's parts.
3. **Constraints.** `May change:` covers the texts the change makes wrong by their directories (`skills/`, `docs/`, `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`), not as a list of files or parts. No `Never:` line forbids what `May change:` or the Goal's test route needs, such as a new recipe version under `recipes/`.

## Route each question before you ask it

| The question is | Its place | Ask the owner? |
|---|---|---|
| a fact about the code, the stores or the history | look it up yourself or with a subagent; check a subagent's fact before you rely on it | never |
| a choice between options a run could separate | a DesignQuestion with at least two rival Hypotheses, and the scenario that separates them in the body; this holds also when the owner settles it in the grill | never as a choice; ask only whether the run should test it |
| what the purpose must allow or must never allow | a line of the Goal | yes |
| the purpose, its scope, who asked and why | the Goal's title and body | yes |
| what a run may change, may only read, or must never do | the Goal body's `May change:`, `Read only:` and `Never:` headings | yes |
| how the tree is run (process, review, order, cadence) | the Goal body, an Experiment's verdict rule, or the `/goal` prompt; never a line | only where it is a preference |
| a purpose outside this Goal | a separate Goal, added by the owner | name it; the owner decides |

A testable option set is never put to the owner as a choice. If the owner settles such a question in the session anyway, it is still a DesignQuestion with its rivals, recorded as decided with the session as evidence (see Writes), so the tree says it was argued, not tested. A question becomes a DesignQuestion only when you can name the scenario a run would execute to separate its rivals, such as two Goals in one store, or a base that moves mid-run. A decision with alternatives but no such scenario, such as a preferred shape, bound or word, is the owner's: it is a line or body text, never a question recorded as decided. One DesignQuestion holds one question, and every rival under it answers that question; two grill questions are two DesignQuestions.

## The derivation guard

Before you propose any stored field, flag or event, ask: can replay derive this from the log at that position? If it can, do not propose it. A stored copy of a derived fact, such as a relation label beside a key or a role beside an actor, can disagree with what it copies. This mistake recurs more than any other in a design grill; check it on every field, before the owner has to.

## Derive the lines

Lines are the Goal's positive and negative space, written once and never edited.

- **One line per invariant, not per feature.** List each state the purpose must allow (positive, `[P]`) and each state it must never allow (negative, `[N]`).
- **Negative space comes from what the grill rejected.** Each rejected option that would produce a reachable state is a forbidden state, so it is an `[N]` line. A rejected option that is only a shape, such as an unknown field a strict decoder already refuses, gives no line.
- **Merge states one invariant guards.** At most 10 lines of 1 to 600 runes each; the cap forces the merging.
- **A line carries its own cases.** A line that compares output with a baseline names the baseline by sha256 and asserts that it differs from the candidate; other lines name no baseline. Name each exception it allows in its own words, not only in a later prompt.
- **A line may cite settled keys** (`--cite N=KEY`): a line, an accepted or closed limit, an answered reading, or a selected or contradicted Hypothesis.

**For a build Goal** (the candidate is a commit), a line asserts one property of the candidate, checked by its own tests or one pinned instrument. `[P]` pins what a valid input produces, exactly. `[N]` pins that the forbidden state is refused at write, with exit 1 and a message that names the rule, and that a log holding it is rejected on replay. Before you write a line, it must pass six questions. Does it:

1. name only the candidate's behaviour?
2. get decided by the candidate's tests or one pinned instrument?
3. use an input that can be built on the candidate?
4. need only runner acts on the branch?
5. state one invariant in the P or N form?
6. fail on some commit that could be named?

A line that names history ("fails on the commit before"), the process, an owner act or a reading fails. Red on base, the removal check and "each rule has a test pair" are facts about the tests, so they go in each Experiment's verdict rule, never in a line. A runner cannot meet a line about history, and it will stop on it.

**For a discovery Goal** (the candidate is a claim, measured by a recipe and a rubric), a line names a case every candidate must meet that a check can run on every candidate.

**A Goal whose questions are all settled by argument in the session** (a design record) gets no lines: no run checks its candidates, so a line there is owed forever. Its cases go to the lines of the Goal that builds the design.

## Split purposes into Goals

hyp owes every line on every top-level question that has a candidate. So draw a grid: lines down the side, top-level questions across, and in each cell ask "could one run cover every candidate of this question for this line?" A cell no run could ever fill means the question and the line serve different purposes: put them in separate Goals. A quick proxy: group the top-level questions by what their candidate is (a claim argued with stand-ins, a commit in repository X, a commit in repository Y). Each group is one Goal. A design record and the build of that design are two Goals.

## Before the round closes

1. **A second reader.** Ask an independent reviewer, such as a fresh subagent on the strongest model, to walk every settled rule through a scenario the grill did not draw: two Goals in one store, a merged log from two actors, a base that moves mid-run. Give it the rules and the code, not your conclusion. Check each fact it reports against the source before you rely on it.
2. **Apply the model to itself.** If the Goal changes the tool or rules that will judge it, check its lines against that change.
3. **A preflight scan.** Read every store and text the change touches for a claim the run would contradict, such as a design that says "no store holds X" while one does. Each owner decision a scan can raise is asked now, not by the run.

## Confirm the routing

Run the mistakes checklist on the table first. Before any write, show the owner one table with a row per grill question: the question, where it goes (line, Goal body, DesignQuestion with its rivals, looked up, another Goal), and for a DesignQuestion the scenario that separates its rivals. Mark each line `[P]` or `[N]` and the invariant it states. The owner confirms each row or moves it. Which settled questions the tree records as DesignQuestions is the owner's call; the table is where they make it. Write nothing before they confirm.

## Writes

The grill ends in these writes, in this order. Show each owner write as the exact command with the owner's actor name; run it only after the owner approves that command in the session. Their approval is the owner's act; you only type it. Never write under the owner's name without it.

| Output | Command | Actor |
|---|---|---|
| a new store, if none exists | `hyp init` | runner |
| the Goal, its purpose and its lines | `hyp add goal --title "…" --body "…" --line "…" --cite N=KEY --why "…"` | owner |
| a contested question | `hyp add dq --parent <G-id> …`, then one `hyp add hyp --parent <Q-id> …` per rival | runner |
| a question with rivals the owner settled in the session | the DesignQuestion and each rival as above; then under the chosen rival `hyp add exp --recipe none --rubric reading --target <each other rival>` whose body states the scenarios as its rule, `hyp record` with a verdict per rival citing a scenarios file under `.tree/evidence/<E-id>/`, then the select OWED owes (a runner write, not the owner's) | runner |

| the end | `hyp checkpoint --goal <G-id> --summary "…" --why "end of grill"` | runner |

The Goal body ends with the run's constraints block, so a run and `hyp prompt` can find it:

```text
May change: <the repository, how it is changed (for example commits on one local branch, a PR never merged), and the texts the change makes wrong>
Read only: <repositories, directories or data the run may read but never change>
Never: <acts the run never takes, such as replacing an installed binary or publishing source data>
```

The block runs from the first line that starts with `May change:`, `Read only:` or `Never:` to the end of the body. It holds each of the three headings at least once, and every non-empty line in it starts with one of them, so write one constraint per line and put no other text after the block. A line of spaces, a tab or a lone carriage return is not empty: leave a blank line truly empty, and write the body with `\n` line ends. A heading may repeat, such as one `Never:` line per act. `hyp add goal` warns when a body has a heading but no valid block, and `hyp prompt` refuses that Goal.

A body that names another tree's ids writes each as `<tree>:<id>`. Then run `hyp status <G-id>` and `hyp check`: it must print `check: 0 errors`. Commit `.tree/events/` and `.tree/evidence/`.

## Hand off

hyp prints the `/goal` prompt for hyp-goal-run from the log. Choose a new runner actor, then run:

```text
hyp prompt <G-id> --actor <runner-actor> [--branch <branch>] [--pr <N>] [--experiments <N>]
```

It prints the store's path, the actor, the Goal id, the skill, the stop clauses (the runner owes nothing, or N Results under the actor, 5 by default) and the Goal body's constraints block, line for line; `--branch` and `--pr` add a clause each after the block. Give the owner its output as it is, and do not add to it. The prompt carries no owner answer: OWED lists each answer and each returned limit the runner applies. The practice of a run, a build Goal's review round included, is in hyp-goal-run. Run `hyp prompt` on the log the run starts from: the prompt names the Goal by its id, so the Goal's add must be in that log, merged or on the branch the prompt names. If `hyp prompt` refuses (exit 1), the Goal body has no valid constraints block; a Goal is never edited, so tell the owner, who adds a new Goal with a valid block. Exit 2 is a bad argument, such as a `--branch` with a space; exit 3 means no repository holds the store, so run it from the store inside its repository.

## Never

- Put a testable choice to the owner as a choice.
- Propose a stored field replay can derive.
- Write a line about history, process, an owner act or a reading.
- Add a purpose this Goal does not hold as a line; it is a new Goal.
- Write under the owner's actor without their approval of the exact command.
- End the grill with a question only the owner can answer still in chat and not in the tree.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

1	# Issue #141: Run practice: the last candidate of a budget-bound run goes unreviewed
2	
3	Opened by dat9uy at 2026-11-12T02:21:06Z. Text as of 2026-11-12T03:45:00Z.
4	
5	## Event
6	
7	On 2026-11-12, run 1 of `investigations/goal-prompt` (G-ZBM2RE, PR #140) stopped with its last candidate, H-YXSJEM at `5c5902d`, never reviewed. The two earlier candidates were reviewed, and each review found real defects (10 findings on `10566d4`, 8 on `b4f23b2`). The stop checkpoint says "all review limits closed" and does not name the missing review.
8	
9	The chain, from the run's transcript and the two trees:
10	
11	1. A review finding that is a case of a line becomes a limit, and `--limit` exists only on `hyp record`. So the runner recorded each review as its own Experiment: E-C3GGGJ reviewed `10566d4` and E-7QQ2DP reviewed `b4f23b2`.
12	2. Each candidate therefore cost two Experiments, a gate and a review. The run spent E-HQWTA0, E-C3GGGJ, E-Z5BTZR, E-7QQ2DP and E-NZR3GV (the gate of `5c5902d`), and the stop clause "5 Experiments have been recorded" ended it.
13	3. The default of 5 was set from G-D1CH1R's runs, where every Experiment gates a commit and review findings went straight into fix commits (one Experiment per candidate; run 5 used 4).
14	4. At 17:21:37 the runner wrote "E5 is the last Experiment the budget allows, so this fix commit must close everything." `skills/hyp-goal-run/SKILL.md` asks for "one review of each candidate commit's diff" before the stop. The prompt's stop clause and the skill conflict, and neither says which yields or that the gap is named at the stop.
15	
16	## Scope
17	
18	Core: the run practice of a Goal whose candidate is a commit (review, budget and stop report) in `hyp-goal-run`, and the stop clause `hyp prompt` prints. No self-review recipe is involved.
19	
20	## Rivals
21	
22	A tree holds this question; each option below is a rival Hypothesis, not a decision. The scenario that separates them: replay the G-ZBM2RE cut after R-8JQPWG (one Experiment left, a fix commit pending) and see whether the run stops with every candidate reviewed or with the gap named.
23	
24	- **H-one-experiment:** a candidate's review is part of its gate Experiment. One Result carries the test verdicts and the review's limits, so a candidate costs one Experiment again.
25	- **H-name-at-stop:** keep the practice; the stop checkpoint names each candidate without a review, so the gap is visible to the owner.
26	- **H-reserve-last:** when one Experiment remains, the runner reviews the current candidate instead of committing another fix, and stops with recorded limits.
27	- **H-raise-budget:** the default of `--experiments` rises (for example to 7) to fit a gate and a review per candidate.
28	
29	These can combine (H-name-at-stop with any other); the tree should say which hold alone.
30	
31	## Done means
32	
33	- A tree under this issue selects a rival, or a combination, from a run on the scenario above.
34	- After the change, a run that reaches its budget either has a review Result for its final candidate or names that candidate as unreviewed in the stop checkpoint.

1	---
2	name: hyp-goal-run
3	description: "Run a hyp tree under an owner's Goal and met rule as an unattended /goal, for a discovery Goal or a build Goal: act only on what OWED says the runner owes, test before asking, write readings the owner can answer, reassess the targets under the owner's answers, and stop with a report the owner can read from hyp status. Use when a /goal prompt names this skill, such as the one hyp prompt prints."
4	---
5	
6	The `/goal` prompt names the tree, your actor, the Goal, the stop and the Goal body's constraints; `hyp prompt <goal-id> --actor <actor>` prints it from the log. This skill says how to work until that stop. Use it with the hyp-prototype skill, which says how to add Questions, Hypotheses, Experiments and Results, and the hyp-verification skill, which says how to run an Experiment.
7	
8	## Start
9	
10	- Read the Goal first with `hyp show <goal-id>`, including its checkpoints, because `hyp status` does not print its met rule.
11	- Everything you need is in the tree. Do not read session logs, reports or memory about earlier runs.
12	- The Goal's body states the run's constraints under three headings: `May change:` (what you may write, and how), `Read only:` (what you may read but never change) and `Never:` (acts you never take). Obey them. A `/goal` prompt may narrow them, never widen them. If a step needs something they forbid, refer it with a reason or record a reading, and stop.
13	- A store may hold many Goals. Then `hyp status` prints only a GOALS table and one Awaiting owner list, so run `hyp status <goal-id>` wherever this skill says `hyp status`: OWED, LINES, the stop line and the last checkpoint are per Goal. Name the Goal with `--goal <goal-id>` on `hyp checkpoint`.
14	- Print `hyp status` at the end of every turn.
15	
16	## Work
17	
18	Act on what OWED in `hyp status` says the runner owes, and on nothing else. Plan only the next Experiment.
19	
20	- Use the Goal's must-fail cases as known-answer flaw cases, in the owner's terms.
21	- The recipe's checks may exist before the verdict rule, because `hyp add exp` pins them. Write and run no candidate until the rule is recorded on the Experiment.
22	- Try a new or changed check only on its cases' stand-ins, never on a candidate, until the rule is recorded. If a candidate shows a check is wrong anyway, do not just fix the check: write the case that shows it, in the Goal's terms with the outcome it must give, in a new version, and name that case in the Experiment body. A sentence that discloses a trial run pins nothing.
23	- `hyp record` and `hyp check` warn when a Result's text disagrees with its cited files: a verdict that a cited `verdict:` line contradicts, or a commit or hash in the observation or a limit that no cited file holds. Fix each one with a new Result that cites the file; a Result cannot change after it is recorded.
24	
25	## Build Goals
26	
27	A build Goal's candidate is a commit. Its practice:
28	
29	- Each commit you test is one Hypothesis under the Goal's question, with the branch and the commit in its title. Tie its subject before the run with `hyp subject <H> --base <commit>`. A fix is a new commit and a new Hypothesis that supersedes the old one (`hyp supersede <new> --old <old>`).
30	- Write the tree with the installed hyp. Compile the candidate to a separate path, and never replace an installed binary.
31	- Pin the gate as a recipe when the repository keeps one, so a script decides the verdict. When none does, the Experiment on a commit uses `--recipe none --rubric reading`: its body states the gate as the rule, and the Result cites the gate's logs.
32	- Before you run anything, write each Experiment's verdict rule in its body: the Goal's lines it aims at, red on the base and green on the candidate for each new test, a removal check for each refusal (remove the refusal and show which test fails), and `go vet ./...` and `go test ./... -count=1`, or the repository's own gate. For skill text, run the original and the candidate skills on the same eval cases.
33	- Keep the logs under `.tree/evidence/<E-id>/` and cite them in the Result.
34	- Before the stop, ask a fresh subagent for one review of each candidate commit's diff against the design and the Goal's lines. Give it the code, the lines and the keys already settled, with the owner's words; do not give it your conclusion. Ask it to label each finding with the line it is a case of, or none.
35	- Sort each finding: a case of a line is a `--limit` you close or, only if void, refer; a question about a line's meaning is a reading; a defect in text you may edit is a fix commit; anything else is an out-of-Goal finding, named in the stop checkpoint, and it never holds the select.
36	- The run may push its branch and open or update one PR. It never merges.
37	
38	## Before a trade-off
39	
40	Before a Question goes to the owner as a trade-off, add one structure that is not among the candidates, and the cheapest variant of each contradicted rival that would hold. Run them through a new version of the pinned recipe and record the Result. If a new structure holds every check, say in a checkpoint that the rule does not decide this Question.
41	
42	## Readings
43	
44	- When a verdict rests on your reading of a Goal line, write the other reading as a strict check: a separate named command in the recipe, with its own known answers, that sets no verdict. Say so in the Experiment's verdict rule, and run it on the same candidates. Record the reading with `hyp record --reading`, naming the check and which candidates fail it. If the recipe cannot test the other reading, say that in the reading.
45	- When a verdict rests on the word of a reading that is still open under AWAITING OWNER, or on an owner answer another Result already reads, record the same reading on that Result too, word for word, with the same `--reading-of` key if it has one: a reading holds only its own Result's Question, and hyp prints identical readings as one question and warns when the owner answers only one. Record a copy only on a Result that judged a Hypothesis whose verdict differs from the strict check's outcome for it: a `supports` the check fails, or a `contradicts` the check passes. A Result whose judged Hypotheses the check gives the same outcome as the verdict gets no copy. The owner answers every copy in one answer, because `--answer` is repeatable.
46	- Before you record a reading, look for a test that can decide it. If a test fits the Goal's lines, write it, run it under the verdict rule, and record no reading. If a test needs a new Goal line, name the test, the fact it measures and the line in the reading, and ask the owner whether to run it. Ask the owner to choose a meaning only when no test can decide, and say why none can.
47	- Write each reading in ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English: short sentences, active verbs, one meaning for each word, and the Goal's words for things. Use this form:
48	
49	  ```text
50	  <Goal line>: "<the words>" has two meanings. Meaning 1: <...>. Meaning 2: <...>. This run used meaning <n>. <Check> tests meaning <n>; <candidates> fail it. Question: <one question the owner can answer in their own words>?
51	  ```
52	
53	  Give one small example of each meaning, in the Goal's terms. If the line does not have two meanings, state the case it does not clearly cover, then the question. A reading holds at most 600 characters.
54	
55	## Owner answers
56	
57	- When the owner answers a reading, record it with their exact words, `hyp answer --answer "<R-id>#r<n>=<their words>" --actor <owner-actor>`, and treat their answer as the meaning of that line. If the owner's words answer a reading but do not name it, ask which reading before you write; an answer must name its key. Do not leave a question only in chat.
58	- If the owner's answer itself has two meanings, record a reading of that answer with `hyp record --reading-of <R-id>#r<n>="<the form above>"`. It narrows the answer and never reopens it; the answer stays in force.
59	- Only the owner changes an answer. When they give new words for a reading they already answered, record them with the same `hyp answer --answer "<R-id>#r<n>=<their new words>"`; hyp derives that it is a revision. The earlier answer and the Results that applied it stay. Apply the new answer with a Result that `--applies` it, and test a successor (`hyp supersede`) of any Hypothesis the old answer contradicted.
60	- A limit the owner accepts is recorded with `hyp answer --accept "<key>=<their words>" --actor <owner-actor>`, and a return with `--returns`. hyp admits an accept only of a limit you referred, and never under your actor.
61	
62	## Reassess
63	
64	Apply each answered reading that `hyp status` lists under OWED as `apply answer`, and act on each limit it lists.
65	
66	1. For each answer, write one line: the owner's words, the check, and the candidates that fail it. If the owner is in this session, show the lines and wait for their yes. If not, write the lines in the Experiment's body.
67	2. For each Question, add one Experiment that names each answer it applies with `--aims`, and fix how its verdicts are decided before you run it: a rubric from `rubrics/` (`--rubric <name>@<version>`, a new rubric version when the answer changes the rule) or `--rubric reading` with the rule in its body. A recipe measures and never prints a verdict. To reassess records an earlier run kept, pin them with `--records .tree/evidence/<E-id>` and `--recipe none`. If an outcome is already known, say so in the rule. Give a verdict on every target, `inconclusive` when the run could not decide. Record its Result with `--applies` for each answer it applied. Old Results stay as they are.
68	3. If applying an answer raises a new question about what a Goal line or the owner's answer means, record it with `hyp record --reading` on that Result. A Result cannot change after it is recorded, so if it is already recorded, record a new Result under the same Experiment.
69	4. Act on each `limit` line under OWED, whichever Hypothesis its Result gave a verdict on: a limit is a case the Goal covers that no check ran. If a test within the Goal's lines can run the case on every candidate, add an Experiment with `--aims` at it, run it, and record `--closes` on the Result that ran the case. A close records that the case ran, whatever the verdicts: a candidate that fails the case is contradicted and the limit is still closed, so never write a rule that closes it only on a pass. A close covers every case the limit's text names; `hyp record` prints that text when it closes. Record each case you did not run as a new `--limit` on the closing Result, and refer that new key when its case is void or outside the Goal's lines. A claim that a case is void, out of scope or covered elsewhere is a limit and a refer, never a sentence in a body or an observation. When that claim rests on your reading of a Goal line, put the reading in the refer's text. Write one case per `--limit`. If no such test can, or the case is void for every candidate, refer it with your reason: `hyp checkpoint --refers "<key>=<why no test within the Goal can close it, or why the case is void>" --why "..."`; hyp refuses a refer with no reason. When the owner returns a referred limit, it is an ordinary `limit` line again.
70	5. End with the candidates left under each Question: none, one, or several, by alias.
71	6. Select only when OWED lists `select` for that Question: `hyp select <Q-id> <H-id> --why "..."`. Never confirm a select. Do not change the Goal or add new structures unless the owner asks.
72	
73	## Goal lines
74	
75	- The Goal's lines are limits keyed on the Goal, `G-<id>#<n>`; `hyp status` prints them under LINES. A Goal's lines come with its add and no later event adds one. If the Goal's body states lines and none is typed, they cannot be added to this Goal: tell the owner, who may add a new Goal with them (`hyp add goal … --line "<line>"`). Do not write them for the owner.
76	- A line is owed as a `limit` on each top-level Question with a candidate no closer covers. Run its case like any limit: aim at it with `--aims G-<id>#<n>`, and record `--closes G-<id>#<n>` on each Result that ran the case. A Result covers a candidate it gave a verdict on, or one whose whole subject (base, patch and files) one of the Result's cited runs holds, so tie each candidate before the run: `hyp subject <H> [PATH…] --base <commit> [--patch FILE]`.
77	- A line is never edited. What a line means is a reading. A line no test within the Goal can run is a refer, and the owner accepts or returns it. A new line or a new purpose is a new Goal, so a new tree: tell the owner, and do not write it.
78	
79	## Stop
80	
81	Stop on the clauses the `/goal` prompt names. Stopping is not success.
82	
83	1. Before your last message, record a runner checkpoint, so the fork does not live only in chat; the owner reads `hyp status`, which prints the last checkpoint, each reading in full and what each copy's answer can touch. Do not restate a reading's meanings in the checkpoint:
84	
85	   ```text
86	   hyp checkpoint --goal <goal-id> --summary "Stopped: <stop clause>. Waiting for the owner: <the keys under AWAITING OWNER>. Out-of-Goal findings: <one short phrase each, or none>" --why "<why>"
87	   ```
88	
89	   An out-of-Goal finding is a case of none of the Goal's lines: it gets no limit, no refer and no reading, and it never holds the select. Name each one in the checkpoint so it lives in the log, not only in chat. A defect in text you changed and may edit is not one: fix it with a commit before the stop.
90	
91	2. Your last message repeats the checkpoint, and lists each line under LINES by its key, with the Results that ran it, and names each question where OWED still owes a line. A run that ends with lines owed is a normal result.
92	
93	3. Then list every owner item with the exact command the owner runs: each item under AWAITING OWNER, each out-of-Goal finding (a new Goal or an issue), merging the PR, reinstalling hyp, and each personal skill that names a command the change altered.
94	
95	## Never
96	
97	- Never change the Goal or its met rule.
98	- Never record a choice the owner reserved, and never record an owner answer unless the owner gave those words in this session.
99

docs/glossary.md:3:The words hyp uses for its tree, its recipes and its sandboxes. The specs ([replay-spec.md](replay-spec.md), [sandbox-spec.md](sandbox-spec.md)) and the recipe format define the rules; this file only fixes which word means what, links the rule's section instead of restating it, and names the Go type that owns each concept where one exists. It also names the two scopes of this repository, core and self-review, and the test that puts an item in one; [core-and-self-review.md](core-and-self-review.md) maps the repository onto them.
docs/glossary.md:46:A Goal whose candidate is a commit: building is a Goal like any other. A line asserts one property of the candidate, decided by its own tests or one pinned instrument: `[P]` pins what a valid input produces, and `[N]` pins that a forbidden state is refused. Each commit is a Hypothesis whose subject is the base plus that commit's change, and a fix is a new Hypothesis that supersedes it. Each Experiment's verdict rule asks for red on base and green on the candidate; the base of the red run's subject is where the build starts, and the Goal records no start commit. A finding of a run's review that is a case of a line is a limit; one that is not is an out-of-Goal finding. A change to a skill is a build Goal too (ADR 0021).
docs/glossary.md:145:_Avoid_: approve, review; verdict (alone: a confirm's answer was a confirm verdict)
docs/glossary.md:155:Retired by ADR 0015. It was the role that confirmed every select, independently of the actor who made it. Old verifier confirms replay as history and apply nothing, and `hyp confirm` is retired (ADR 0019). Any actor may still review: a defect is recorded as a Result, a retract or a limit. In code: `event.RoleVerifier`, read only from old logs.
docs/glossary.md:156:_Avoid_: reviewer, checker (as a role)
docs/glossary.md:179:A finding, often from a run's review, that is a case of none of the Goal's lines and asks no question about what a line means. It is not a limit, since a limit is a case the Goal covers, so it gets no tree event, no refer and no accept, and it never holds the select. The runner names it in its stop checkpoint's summary and its last message as a possible new Goal or issue, and the owner decides at global scope whether to add one. A defect in text the run changed and may edit is not one: the run fixes it with a commit.
docs/glossary.md:438:Every concept hyp has, and everything a user who installs hyp into another repository runs, loads or reads there. A concept stays core when self-review is what tests it.
docs/glossary.md:441:**Self-review**:
docs/glossary.md:442:The recipes this repository keeps to test hyp, whatever repository the runner works on, with the inputs only they use. Investigating hyp is an activity, not a scope: a tree about hyp takes the scope of its question, and a tree about another project is a self-review input.

usage: hyp <command> [flags]

Every write command needs --why and an actor (--actor or $HYP_ACTOR).
Statuses are derived from events; no command can set one.

setup:
  init                                   create .tree in the current directory
  version                                print the hyp version

write:
  add goal --title T [--body B] [--alias A] [--line L]... [--cite N=KEY]...
  add dq   --parent REF --title T [--body B] [--alias A]
  add hyp  --parent REF --title T [--body B] [--alias A] [--subject PATH]...
  add exp  --parent REF --title T --recipe NAME@V|none [--rubric NAME@V|reading] [--records PATH]... [--target REF|none]... [--alias A]
  record   --exp REF [--verdict REF=supports|contradicts|inconclusive]... --observation O [--evidence P]... [--limit L]... [--closes R#N]...
  retract REF | abandon REF | reaffirm REF
  supersede NEW --old OLD
  amend HYP --body B                     revise a Hypothesis body
  subject HYP [PATH...] [--base C]       tie a Hypothesis to the base and files that embody its claim
  link FROM depends_on|external_ref TO   unlink FROM TYPE TO
  select DQ [HYP]                        admitted only when hyp status owes it (no HYP: print the suggestion only)
  unselect DQ | defer DQ | withdraw DQ|EXP | resume DQ
  checkpoint [--summary S] [--goal G] [--refers K[=TEXT]]...   the runner's report: a summary, refers, or both
  answer [--answer R#rN=TEXT]... [--accept K=TEXT]... [--returns K=TEXT]...   the owner's act; no --why

read (REF/TIME: an event id, a node ref, or an RFC3339 time):
  status [--as-of REF|TIME] [--max-lines N] [--live]   orientation screen, 60 lines by default; --live hides contradicted rivals
  show REF|R-id#n|G-id#n [--as-of REF|TIME]  one node, or one limit or line, in full, with its history
  diff --since REF|TIME                       status changes and events since a point
  render --markdown [--as-of REF|TIME]        the whole tree as Markdown, untruncated
  check                                       rejected events, bad lines, warnings
  signals [--json]                            design marks for the whole tree: one-rival, D1
  events --json                               applied events in merge order, and rejected ones, as JSON for scripts
  prompt G-id --actor A [--branch B] [--pr N] [--experiments N]   the /goal prompt for a Goal, from its body's constraints block

bundle (a recipe in recipes/ or a rubric in rubrics/; a name lives in one library):
  bundle hash DIR [--json]               the bundle hash add exp --recipe or --rubric records for DIR
  bundle check                           every pin to a versioned bundle, in every tree under the repo root, still matches it
  bundle new NAME@1 [--rubric]           write a first recipe, or with --rubric a first rubric, beside the nearest .tree/ from hyp's template; fill every hyp:placeholder
  bundle new NAME@N --from NAME@M        copy bundle NAME@M to the next version NAME@N in its library, writing from:
  bundle run --record DIR REF NAME [ARGS...]   run one Standalone command with no sandbox; exits with its exit code
  bundle evidence --record DIR REF OUT_DIR     run recipe REF's Evidence commands on remove's OUT_DIR; exits with the failing one's code
  bundle known-answers REF                     run every known-answers/NAME/ case of bundle REF, twice each; 1 on a wrong answer

sandbox (a disposable clone under ~/.hyp-sandbox/ID for one Experiment):
  sandbox create ID --host H --base REV --recipe NAME@VERSION|none [--recipe NAME@VERSION]... [--recipes DIR] [--store SRC --cut EVENT] [--inputs FILE] [--hyp BIN]
  sandbox drive ID                             run every recipe's Drive commands in the sandbox; exits with the failing one's code
  sandbox remove ID OUT_DIR [--keep REL]... | sandbox remove ID --discard

skills/hyp-owner-grill/SKILL.md:50:- **Merge states one invariant guards.** At most 10 lines of 1 to 600 runes each; the cap forces the merging.
skills/hyp-owner-grill/SKILL.md:113:hyp prompt <G-id> --actor <runner-actor> [--branch <branch>] [--pr <N>] [--experiments <N>]
docs/replay-spec.md:246:- A **pin** is a recipe ref (`name@version`) and the hash an event recorded for it at write time. A bundle is its ref and hash; a `recipes/<name>@<version>/` directory name is only the library's lookup key, and hyp opens each copy it makes by the ref it holds ([ADR 0005](adr/0005-a-bundle-is-its-ref-and-hash.md)). docs/glossary.md:3:The words hyp uses for its tree, its recipes and its sandboxes. The specs ([replay-spec.md](replay-spec.md), [sandbox-spec.md](sandbox-spec.md)) and the recipe format define the rules; this file only fixes which word means what, links the rule's section instead of restating it, and names the Go type that owns each concept where one exists. It also names the two scopes of this repository, core and self-review, and the test that puts an item in one; [core-and-self-review.md](core-and-self-review.md) maps the repository onto them.
docs/glossary.md:46:A Goal whose candidate is a commit: building is a Goal like any other. A line asserts one property of the candidate, decided by its own tests or one pinned instrument: `[P]` pins what a valid input produces, and `[N]` pins that a forbidden state is refused. Each commit is a Hypothesis whose subject is the base plus that commit's change, and a fix is a new Hypothesis that supersedes it. Each Experiment's verdict rule asks for red on base and green on the candidate; the base of the red run's subject is where the build starts, and the Goal records no start commit. A finding of a run's review that is a case of a line is a limit; one that is not is an out-of-Goal finding. A change to a skill is a build Goal too (ADR 0021).
docs/glossary.md:145:_Avoid_: approve, review; verdict (alone: a confirm's answer was a confirm verdict)
docs/glossary.md:155:Retired by ADR 0015. It was the role that confirmed every select, independently of the actor who made it. Old verifier confirms replay as history and apply nothing, and `hyp confirm` is retired (ADR 0019). Any actor may still review: a defect is recorded as a Result, a retract or a limit. In code: `event.RoleVerifier`, read only from old logs.
docs/glossary.md:156:_Avoid_: reviewer, checker (as a role)
docs/glossary.md:179:A finding, often from a run's review, that is a case of none of the Goal's lines and asks no question about what a line means. It is not a limit, since a limit is a case the Goal covers, so it gets no tree event, no refer and no accept, and it never holds the select. The runner names it in its stop checkpoint's summary and its last message as a possible new Goal or issue, and the owner decides at global scope whether to add one. A defect in text the run changed and may edit is not one: the run fixes it with a commit.
docs/glossary.md:438:Every concept hyp has, and everything a user who installs hyp into another repository runs, loads or reads there. A concept stays core when self-review is what tests it.
docs/glossary.md:441:**Self-review**:
docs/glossary.md:442:The recipes this repository keeps to test hyp, whatever repository the runner works on, with the inputs only they use. Investigating hyp is an activity, not a scope: a tree about hyp takes the scope of its question, and a tree about another project is a self-review input.

# One store holds many Goals

Until now a tree had one Goal (spec §5 rule 4: "only one Goal per log"). A new purpose was a new tree, and that tree cited the old one in prose as `<tree>:ID`, which hyp does not check (ADR 0016). After the multi-tenant tree completed on 2026-11-10, the owner wanted the build that follows a tree to run from the tree instead of from a plan in prose. Every problem with that came from the one-Goal rule:

- A build had no checked way to cite what the tree had decided.
- The owner's checkpoints were split across trees.
- A commit could not be a subject, because `hyp record` copied file hashes and dropped the sandbox's `base` (`internal/cli/subject.go:118`).

In session `e6a35a24` (2026-11-10 and 11) the owner settled the model: **building is a Goal like any other.** hyp keeps no discovery kind and no delivery kind. The design questions it raised are recorded and selected in `investigations/checkpoint-store-design` (G-73R704), with that session as evidence:

- Q-D906CD (R-HW9B05): what a Result keeps about its runs.
- Q-HC4V9T (R-V8032Z): where a build Goal's start commit lives.
- Q-H8PJ20 (R-8CJCV6): what the owner's act is attached to.
- Q-R21S8R (R-AWPQ4X): how many event types there are.

`investigations/checkpoint-store` (G-D1CH1R) builds the design, and its nine owner lines are this ADR's acceptance. Tracked in #126, part of #114.

## Decision

- **One store holds many Goals.** The store is still one `.tree/` with one events file per actor. A tree is a view, not a container: a Goal and every node whose parents lead to it. Rule 4's "only one Goal per log" goes.
- **A subject has one shape: a base commit, plus what is given over it.** What is given over it is at most one patch, and input files. This holds for every sense of the word:
  - an Experiment's subject is what its sandbox assembles;
  - a run's subject is the base, the one patch and the input files its records name;
  - a Hypothesis's subject may name a base and at most one patch over it, and names files by sha256.

  A Result keeps **one subject per cited run**, `{base, patch, files}`, instead of one merged `fingerprints` list. A Hypothesis is covered when one entry holds its whole subject, so a run at B plus a patch never covers bare B. An old Result reads as one entry with no base. The word `fingerprints` stays for the hashed files inside a subject (Q-D906CD).

Round 1. The store is `investigations/goal-prompt`, which holds #141's parent Goals G-GZR6C6 (the design record) and G-ZBM2RE (the build). I looked up what I could:

- **What the stop clause counts.** It counts Results recorded under the actor (`internal/cli/prompt.go:167`), not Experiments. The default of 5 comes from `--experiments`.
- **Both cuts can be replayed.** `hyp sandbox create` takes a store cut (`--store SRC --cut EVENT`). The R-8JQPWG record event is in the claude-g113-1 and claude-g113-2 logs, and the three candidate commits are in git history.
- **Why every review costs a Result.** A limit needs a Result and a Result needs an Experiment (glossary, "Limit"; ADR 0018). I won't ask about that.

**1. Is this Goal a design Goal, with the build as a separate Goal later?**
- Today: the issue's "Done means" has two parts. One is to select a rival from a run on the scenario. The other is the changed behaviour after the change, which is edits to `hyp-goal-run` and `hyp prompt`.
- Option A, one design Goal now:
  - Its candidates are rival run rules. Each rule is given to a runner as stand-in text on the cut, and the runner is not a commit.
  - Example: the run replays cut A under H-reserve-last's text and checks where the replay stops.
  - After the select, a build Goal gets its own grill, with lines that quote the selected rule. This is the same split as G-GZR6C6 and G-ZBM2RE.
- Option B, one Goal holding both:
  - Its lines would be about a commit that doesn't exist yet.
  - Every rival would be owed lines about skill text that only the winner gets built into.
- **Recommend A.** A candidate that is a claim and a candidate that is a commit can't share lines.

**2. Do the rivals belong to one question, and is H-whole-candidate in this Goal?**
- Today: the issue lists H-one-experiment, H-name-at-stop, H-reserve-last and H-raise-budget. Your comments add H-probe-closes and H-whole-candidate.
- The first five answer one question: what makes a run reach its stop with its last candidate reviewed or named? Their scenario is the end of a budget-bound run.
- H-whole-candidate answers a different question: what does the review read? On cut A or B it changes no stop, so no line about the stop could separate it. hyp owes every line on every top-level question, so that line would be unfillable.
- Option A:
  - One DesignQuestion with five rivals, and H-whole-candidate as its own Goal, to be added by you.
  - The run adds a combination rival only if no single rival holds on both cuts. This is hyp-goal-run's own "before a trade-off" practice, and it answers the issue's "which hold alone".
- Option B: H-whole-candidate as a second DesignQuestion in this Goal, with a second line "the final candidate's cumulative diff from the base is reviewed". Every rival for the first question would then fail that line.
- **Recommend A.** Do you want it as a separate Goal?

**3. What must a line require at the stop?**
- Today: the issue accepts either end. The final candidate has a review Result, or the stop checkpoint names it as unreviewed.
- Option A, floor only:
  - Line: no candidate is left both unreviewed and unnamed at the stop, on either cut.
  - Every rival meets the floor. They differ on whether a review happened, and several can survive.
  - You choose among the survivors, which is the owner's turn to choose (ADR 0015).
- Option B, "reviewed" as a positive line:
  - H-name-at-stop alone is then contradicted. H-reserve-last is the only way to meet it on cut A, and the lines pick the winner.
- **Recommend A.** It is faithful to "either", and B decides a trade-off for you.

**4. Which lines (all [N] unless marked)?** All three are checked by replay on the two cuts, cut A and cut B, which are listed in question 5.
1. [N] On either cut, the run stops with a candidate commit that has no review Result and is not named as unreviewed in the stop checkpoint.
2. [N] On either cut, the run records more Results under its actor than the stop clause printed for it allows.
3. [P] On either cut, the stop checkpoint and the run's last message state, for each candidate commit, either its review Result or that it has none.

Line 3 is the stop-report side of line 1. Do you want 1 and 3 merged? That would be one invariant with an exception, but it would run to about 400 characters. I'd keep line 3 apart, because line 1 forbids a state and line 3 pins the report. "Say how a review is recorded and whether it counts against the budget" is a line of the build Goal. I'll note it in the Goal body and add it to that Goal.

**5. How is the scenario run? Use ak-skill-creator's eval flow, and with what model, trials and budget?**
- Today: ak-skill-creator owns the test method for skill text: matched original and variant runs on cases.
- The cases are:
  - Cut A: G-ZBM2RE after R-8JQPWG. One Result is left and a fix commit is pending.
  - Cut B: run 3's cut after R-JHBCWS. A probe passed.
- Each rival is a stand-in text for hyp-goal-run (or the printed clause), given to the runner. Nothing under `skills/` is edited.
- **Recommend yes** to the flow. For model, trials and budget: the model that ran your `/goal` runs, 3 trials per rival per cut, and `--experiments 8`. That is one Experiment per rival, one for any combination, and spare room. The default of 5 would stop this run before it finished, which is the issue's own failure.
- Do you accept these, or give your own?

**6. Constraints block (for approval).**
```text
May change: this repository, in commits on the branch the prompt names that follow AGENTS.md; the run may push that branch and open or update one PR, and never merges it. It changes investigations/goal-prompt (.tree/ and its evidence) and may add a new version of a recipe or rubric under recipes/ or rubrics/. It edits no skill, doc or code.
Read only: skills/, docs/, internal/, cmd/, plans/, every other investigations/ tree, and ak-skill-creator under .claude/skills.
Never: commit to main or merge a PR.
Never: replace an installed binary; compile any candidate to a separate path.
Never: edit a frozen recipe or rubric version, another investigations/ tree or another repository.
Never: write under an owner's actor.
```
The change belongs to the build Goal, so `May change:` here lists no skill or doc. Any edit to the texts this rule makes wrong waits for that Goal.

**7. Your actor name.** For example `owner-dat`. I'll use `HYP_ACTOR=claude-grill-141` for my runner writes.

I'll hold the preflight scan and the independent review until you answer. After that I'll send the routing table.

# Context Engineering

Finish the requested work correctly with less wasted context, cost, time and agent
steps. Optimize complete outcomes, including failures, retries and verification.
Never cut required scope or verification to meet an efficiency target.

## Operating loop

1. **Frame:** identify the outcome, constraints and acceptance checks. Reuse an
   accepted plan. Short tasks need no additional plan or ledger ceremony.
2. **Observe:** use available runtime telemetry. Distinguish context occupancy,
   cumulative task spend, provider quota and dollar cost. Missing values are unknown.
3. **Allocate:** reserve room for the next result, response and checkpoint. Reserve
   task budget for verification and integration before assigning independent work.
4. **Execute:** search for the owner, read a sufficient logical unit, bound tool
   output while preserving errors, and record decisions/evidence worth retaining.
5. **Reassess:** expand only when evidence is missing; stop exploration when acceptance
   is met. Checkpoint before a step likely to exceed headroom or when context degrades.

## Proportional hygiene

- Search before large reads (roughly 2k tokens is a hint, not a prohibition).
  Read whole files when their structure or cross-cutting contract is the question.
- Keep a small current-state ledger for long work: observed facts with source/revision,
  decisions with reasons, open uncertainties, and next action. Do not log every read.
- Reuse verified facts until the source, revision, environment or decision changes.
  Refresh changed or consequential live state; line numbers alone are not identity.
- Prefer native output limits or structured filters. For shell logs, preserve the
  producer exit status, retain a full log when necessary, and report truncation.
  Follow the safe pattern in [session protocol](references/session-protocol.md).
- Batch independent bounded calls, inspect every result, and keep dependent operations
  sequential. Limit the aggregate output too; batching is not free context capacity.
- Retry a transient failure within a bounded policy/backoff. For deterministic errors,
  change the cause before retrying. Recheck when relevant state changes.
- Run focused checks first; broaden when required by repository gates or risk.
  Keep useful progress updates; avoid repeating plans and dumping results.
- Load one reference per current question. Instructions from the runtime or project
  still take precedence over this skill's efficiency heuristics.

## Cache and cost observations

When the host exposes them, record input/output tokens, cache reads/writes, elapsed time,
retries and cost per successful task with model/runtime/settings and source identity.
Missing telemetry remains `null`/unknown, never estimated from file length. Context occupancy
is not cumulative billed tokens or currency. Prefix stability, cache policy and reasoning
effort belong to prompt assembly/adapters or APIs; renaming a skill does not establish a
cache improvement. Compare matched original/candidate runs before changing runtime defaults.

## Capacity and task budgets

Context bands are advisory defaults: Green <50%, Yellow 50–<70%, Orange 70–<85%,
Red ≥85%. They are not calibrated quality thresholds for every model. Available
headroom and the next atomic step matter more than the band. Unknown telemetry
never becomes a percentage based on twenty or forty tool calls.

At Orange or insufficient headroom, finish a safe atomic boundary, checkpoint,
then use a supported compaction capability. In Red, prioritize recovery and the
checkpoint over new exploration. Never abandon a required safety check. If no
compaction tool is available, preserve continuation state without claiming to have
compacted or creating a new session without authorization.

Details: [runtime awareness](references/runtime-awareness.md),
[session protocol](references/session-protocol.md).

## Model selection and delegation

Keep all four core metrics: **Average cost per task**, **Average task duration**,
**Estimated cost per successful first attempt**, **Average agent steps**.
First require sufficient task-specific success and capability. Then compare
cost per first-attempt success and duration; use raw cost for budget planning and
steps to diagnose waste. Do not blend correlated metrics into an arbitrary score.

Compare model + effort + harness on matched task cohorts with dated provenance.

Delegate only when independent work or context isolation justifies startup, duplicated

Packet: task, exact read/owned paths, acceptance, decisions/constraints, allocated

## Checkpoint contract

Merge current state into an existing authorized plan/note; do not retain a growing
archive of stale facts. Preserve intent and verbatim constraints; files/revisions;
decisions and reasons; commands/results; uncertainties/failures; next safe action.
Keep open items explicitly unverified. Retain source pointers for necessary details.
After compaction, read the note and recheck state that could have changed. Do not
assume one passing check validates every claim. For cross-session continuation use
an installed handoff capability. [Compression contract](references/context-compression.md).

## Tools and deeper references

Run scripts from this skill's resolved directory with an available Python 3 runtime.
All utilities are offline; `--help` describes inputs. They do not change runtime settings.

- `scripts/context_analyzer.py estimate <paths> [--limit N]`: approximate file sizes.
- `scripts/context_analyzer.py analyze <messages.json> [--limit N] [--used-tokens N]`:
  capacity and lexical diagnostics; no measured health or poisoning score.
- `scripts/context_analyzer.py budget`: separate window and cumulative task accounting.
- `scripts/compression_evaluator.py`: lexical diagnostics or explicitly supplied grading.
- `scripts/benchmark_metrics.py`: aggregate supplied run records, not run models.

Additional references: [fundamentals](references/context-fundamentals.md),
[optimization](references/context-optimization.md), [degradation](references/context-degradation.md),

[pipelines](references/project-development.md). Reasoning depth:

**Your answers**
- **Q2:** Yes, that is option A. All five rivals go under one question and all are tested. H-whole-candidate is a separate Goal that you add, and it is the expected loser on cost. That Goal can later cite line 6 below.

- **Q6, no push and no PR:** this applies to the grill only. I'll commit the grill's writes locally and push nothing. The constraints block stays as written, so the run itself may push its branch and open one PR.

**What ak-context-engineering gives and doesn't give**
- It gives three rules I'll use:
  1. Cost comes from observed telemetry only. A missing value stays unknown and is never estimated.
  2. Original and candidate runs are matched by task and trial id.
  3. Failed and timed-out trials are recorded as rows.
- It does not give a median or a hang rule. Its aggregator reports averages, so those two rules are the Goal's own, as you said.

**The two cuts**
- Cut A is the record event of R-8JQPWG, `01M75T1YRF2R2Z99DX0E8JQPWG`. Four Results are recorded under the runner, so one is left.
- Cut B is the record event of R-JHBCWS, `01M76VXNN2ZW5WAXJ194JHBCWS`. Four Results are left.
- Each trial runs forward from its cut to the stop. No trial replays a whole build.

**4. Lines, with your two aims**
1. [N] On cut A or cut B, a trial stops with a candidate commit that has no review Result and is not named as unreviewed in the stop checkpoint.
2. [N] On either cut, a trial records more Results under its actor than the stop clause it was given allows.
3. [P] On either cut, the stop checkpoint and the last message give, for each candidate commit, its review Result or say it has none.
4. [P] On either cut, in every one of the 3 Sonnet trials, the final candidate has a review Result before the stop clause ends. This is your first aim, that a review must not easily run out of the budget.
5. [N] On either cut, a trial commits a candidate whose diff changes only tests or spec text for a case its own probe already passed on the previous candidate. This is your second aim, no endless review over small changes. It is run 2's `3cfd08d` and run 3's `d2d5d14` and `04142f3`.
6. [N] On either cut, a candidate's median trial cost is above 1.5 times the base's median at that cut. This is the cost limit; the numbers are below.

- **Line 5:** a trial breaks it only when the commit's diff touches no non-test Go file and no skill, and a passing probe log for that case exists on the previous candidate. A commit that fixes a real defect is not a case of line 5. Is that the right edge?

**Cost for line 6, my proposal**
- **Unit:** tokens the Sonnet runner used from the cut to the stop. That is input, output, cache read and cache write, summed, as the eval harness observes them. I prefer tokens to dollars because a price table changes. Results are already bounded by line 2, and wall time depends on the machine. A trial with no observed tokens is invalid and is re-run, never estimated.
- **Median:** each rival and the base run 3 trials per cut. Sort the 3 costs and take the middle one. One hang therefore doesn't move the median. Two hangs make the median the greatest cost.
- **Hang:** a trial with no stop checkpoint after 30 minutes. Its cost is the greatest cost seen at that cut, across the base and every rival. A hang also fails lines 1 and 4 by itself.

The reviewer infers that the host's local branch `work`, with all the later fix commits, stays in the clone. I read the code but did not run a clone, so this is likely, not confirmed. I'll make the run check it.

My earlier line 6 named no baseline hash and left "review Result" undefined. The reviewer found both. It also found that a trial with no stop silently passed lines 1, 3 and 4. All seven lines are at most 485 runes.
